title: MUSA 5500 Results
text:
Introduction

HB 2186 would allow an ADU (backyard home) on every home lot in Pennsylvania
Legal does not mean built. Philadelphia has allowed ADUs in parts of the city since 2012 and only about 10 were built legally
This half of the project asks four things

Where are people and jobs growing?
Did that change after 2019?
Where would a new ADU pay for itself?
How many ADUs could be built by 2031, under today’s rules and under HB 2186?

Unit: 2020 census tracts (3,445) and towns (2,572 county subdivisions)

title: MUSA 5500 Results
text:
Methods (short)
Full detail is in methods. In short:

01: ACS 2010-14 and 2015-19 moved from 2010 to 2020 tracts with the block crosswalk. Counts by land-area share, medians from the biggest-overlap tract. Dollars in 2024 terms (CPI-U). Yearly growth before and after 2019 for people, homes, jobs, and real rent
02: K-means on six growth rates (jobs, people, rent, before and after)
03: developed share of land per tract from NLCD 2010, 2019, 2025 (zonal stats). Jobs within 30 minutes by car with OSMnx (Philadelphia. Harrisburg could not be downloaded)
04: rent vs cost test for a 600 sq ft ADU. Random forest for housing growth 2010-2020 with spatial cross-validation. ADUs by 2031 per town, scaled from the Pew range of 26 to 81 ADU permits per 100,000 people per year

title: MUSA 5500 Results
text:
Conclusion

Demand: job growth slowed after 2019 across most of PA. Rent growth also slowed in real terms, but one tract group (871 tracts) saw rents speed up
Payoff: a new ADU pays for itself at today’s rates and a $250 / sq ft build cost in only about 20% of tracts, mostly in Philadelphia and its suburbs. Cost matters more than rent
Forecast: HB 2186 could mean about 16,900 ADUs by 2031 (8,200 to 25,500). That is about 3,400 a year, near the low end of what permissive cities see
Under today’s rules the number is much smaller, but that depends on how the ~2,560 uncoded towns are treated

title: MUSA 5500 Results
text:
Limits

ACS tract data is noisy, and the 2020-24 ACS uses a new population base. Population speed-up after 2019 is partly an artifact
The 2010 to 2020 crosswalk uses land area, not where people live
The payoff test uses median rent for all renters. A new ADU may rent for more. It ignores rising build costs, land, permits, and taxes on the new value
The forecast factors (payoff weights, rule factors, demand range) are judgment calls. They are written at the top of notebook 04 so they are easy to change
The town rule list has 9 towns. Coding more towns would change the “today” numbers the most
Lots with room come from MUSA 6950. Its suburban and rural fit rates rest on few pilot tracts, and the fit rule counts front yards

title: MUSA 5500 Data
text:
Notes

Latest year is different for each source. ACS 2020-24, population 2025, jobs 2024, permits 2025, migration 2022-23, land cover 2025.
Tracts changed in 2020. ACS 2014 and 2019 use 2010 tracts. Move them to 2020 tracts with the block crosswalk (TAB2010_TAB2020_ST42.zip).
LODES8 is already on 2020 blocks. No crosswalk needed.
Permits are by town (township, borough, city), not tract. 99% of permit towns match the 2020 town map.
Philadelphia is both a city and a county. Population for Philadelphia comes from the county row.
Migration is by county only and counts tax filers.
ACS rent = median gross rent of all renters, including long-time tenants. It is lower than the rent a new ADU would get.
Census uses -666666666 for “no data”. The script turns these into blanks.
Dollar values need inflation adjustment to 2024 dollars before comparing years. CPI-U yearly average: 2014 = 236.736, 2019 = 255.657, 2024 = 313.689.

title: Backyard Homes PA
text:
The project
A state bill, HB 2186, would allow one accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on every home lot in Pennsylvania. No one knows how many lots have room for one, or where one would pay off. This project answers both, for the whole state.

Is it allowed? Town rules today vs HB 2186
Does it fit? MUSA 6950. AI on aerial images finds open yard space and trees
Does it pay off? MUSA 5500. Population, jobs, rent, and building trends since 2010
How many by 2031? Both halves together

Open the tool

Sent by email, Nov 5, 2026.
To: Prof. Xiaojiang Li, cc TA Zhanchao Yang. Subject: [MUSA550] Final Project Proposal – Ye Zhang
Topic: Housing Demand and ADU Potential Across Pennsylvania
Team: Ye Zhang
Background: A state bill, HB 2186, would allow a backyard home (ADU) on every home lot in Pennsylvania. But legal doesn’t mean built. Philadelphia has allowed ADUs in parts of the city since 2012, and only about 10 have been built legally. ADUs get built where demand is growing and the rent covers the cost.
Research question: Where are people and jobs growing, did that change after 2019, where would an ADU pay off, and how many could be built by 2031?
Study area: All of Pennsylvania, from 2010 to the latest year, by census tract.
Goal: Planners can see where housing demand is growing and how many new homes ADUs could add in their town or county. Builders and homeowners can search an address and see whether an ADU would pay off there.
Data sources: Census population estimates and ACS through the Census API. IRS migration, LEHD jobs, the Building Permits Survey, and Freddie Mac mortgage rates through scripted downloads. NLCD land cover rasters, OpenStreetMap, and lot counts from my 6950 project (or a simpler estimate from lot sizes if those aren’t ready).
Methods:

Join all the data to census tracts.
Compare growth before and after 2019.
Group places by trend with K-means.
Measure developed land from the rasters and job access with OSMnx.
Test where ADU rent covers the cost to build.
Use a random forest to predict where housing grew from 2010 to 2020, then use it to estimate how many ADUs could be built by 2031, with a low and high range.

Expected outcomes: A multi-page Quarto site on GitHub Pages with interactive maps, a time slider from 2010 to today, and a toggle between current rules and HB 2186. A short written report and a presentation.
Course requirements: API collection, 3+ data sources, spatial joins, OSMnx, K-means clustering, raster analysis, and a scikit-learn model, plus interactive visualizations.
How it splits from 6950: My 6950 project uses AI on aerial images to find which lots have room for an ADU. This project covers demand and payoff. The two will share one dashboard, but each has its own code and documentation pages.

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text: Six steps. Each step is one notebook in musa5500/notebooks/. Each notebook saves one table that the tool reads.

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
1. Put everything on 2020 tracts
Notebook 01_trends.ipynb

Counts (people, housing units): move 2010-tract numbers to 2020 tracts by land-area share, using the block crosswalk
Medians (rent, value, income): cannot add them up. Use the value from the 2010 tract with the biggest overlap
Towns: tracts are split into towns with the LODES block crosswalk (block to tract and town), weighted by workers who live in each block (LODES 2024). This replaced the planned center-point join, because many small boroughs are smaller than a tract and would get no tract at all
Inflation: rent and value in 2024 dollars

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
2. Growth before and after 2019
Notebook 01_trends.ipynb

Before = 2010-14 to 2015-19 (ACS) or 2010 to 2019 (jobs)
After = 2015-19 to 2020-24 (ACS) or 2019 to 2024 (jobs)
Yearly growth rate = (end / start)^(1 / years) - 1
Change in trend = growth after - growth before

Positive = sped up
Negative = slowed down

Measures: population, housing units, jobs, rent
A rate is blank if the start is under 200 people, 100 homes, or 50 jobs (tiny bases give wild rates)
growth_before, growth_after, trend_change use population. Each measure also has its own columns (jobs_growth_before, etc.)
Output: data/processed/trends_tract.csv. Notebook 01 also saves tract_panel.csv (all years on 2020 tracts) for notebook 04

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
3. Group places by trend (K-means)
Notebook 02_groups.ipynb

Features: growth before + growth after for jobs, population, and rent
Clip each feature to its 1st and 99th percentile, so a few tiny tracts do not get their own group
Scale with StandardScaler, then KMeans (n_init=10, random_state=42)
Pick k with the elbow method (try 3 to 8), plus silhouette scores. Chose k = 5
Group names are given by profile (highest population growth after 2019, highest job growth after, and so on), so they do not depend on cluster numbers
Name each group in plain words (e.g. “Growing faster”, “Steady”, “Shrinking”)
Output: adds trend_group to trends_tract.csv

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
4. Land and job access
Notebook 03_land_access.ipynb

Developed land: share of each tract in NLCD classes 21-24, for 2010, 2019, 2025

rasterstats.zonal_stats(tracts, tif, categorical=True)

Job access: jobs reachable within 30 minutes by car, from each tract center

OSMnx drive network per metro area, not the whole state (too big)
Scope cut to two areas that hold a MUSA 6950 pilot county: Philadelphia city and Harrisburg (Cumberland + Dauphin). The other metros were left out to keep run time and Overpass load bounded
On the Nov 10 2026 run the public Overpass server was full for hours. Philadelphia downloaded. Harrisburg did not and is skipped until the notebook is rerun
Only the largest strongly connected part of each network is used
Network = metro counties plus a 15 km buffer, clipped to Pennsylvania. Jobs past the buffer or in New Jersey and Delaware are missed
Speeds are posted or default speeds. No traffic
Add speeds and travel times, then Dijkstra from each tract’s nearest node, cutoff 1800 s
Sum LODES 2024 block jobs (WAC) at reachable nodes. Block lat/lon from pa_xwalk.csv.gz
Use networkx, not pandana (pandana is AGPL)

Output: data/processed/access_tract.csv (dev_2010, dev_2019, dev_2025, high-intensity shares, jobs_30min, metro)
Developed share = developed pixels / land pixels (open water left out)

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
5. Does an ADU pay off?
Notebook 04_payoff_forecast.ipynb

Unit: 600 sq ft detached ADU
Cost to build: $175 / $250 / $300 per sq ft (low / mid / high), plus 15% soft costs
Loan: 30 years at the latest Freddie Mac rate
Rent: ACS 2020-24 median gross rent for the tract (2024 dollars) x 1.0. 0.9x and 1.1x are tested
Net rent = rent x (1 - 30%) for vacancy, repairs, tax, insurance
cost_month = payment on the mid cost ($250 / sq ft), all borrowed
pays = yes if net rent >= cost_month. maybe if net rent covers the payment at the low cost ($175 / sq ft) or is within 10% of cost_month. no if below that
Output: data/processed/payoff_tract.csv

title: MUSA 5500 Methods
text:
6. How many ADUs by 2031?
Notebook 04_payoff_forecast.ipynb

Random forest: predict housing growth by tract, 2010 to 2020

Target: 2020 housing units / 2010 housing units (decennial)
Target is log(units 2020 / units 2010). Tracts with under 100 homes in 2010 are left out
Model A: 2010 data only (decennial homes, LODES 2010 jobs and workers, NLCD 2010, land area, location)
Model B: adds ACS 2010-14. Our data has no ACS 2006-10, so this is a small leak. Model B is used only if it beats A by more than 0.02 R2 in spatial CV
Check with random 5-fold CV and spatial CV (whole counties held out). Report R2 and feature importance
The fitted model is then fed 2020 values to rank tracts by expected growth

ADUs by 2031 = people x Pew rate x payoff x lots x demand x rule x 5 years

Pew rate: 26 (low), 53.5 (mid), 81 (high) ADU permits per 100,000 people per year, from cities that allow ADUs
Payoff: yes 1.0, maybe 0.5, no 0.2 (some people build for family, not rent)
Lots: share of homes on a lot with room / state average, capped at 2. From lots_tract.csv (6950) when it exists, else single-family detached share (ACS 2020-24). The notebook switches by itself
Demand: 0.5 to 1.5 from the random forest ranking
Capped at lots with room (fallback: single-family detached homes)

Sanity check: for all of PA the Pew range is about 3,400 to 10,500 a year
Two rules: today (town list in shared/legal_status.csv) and HB 2186 (allowed everywhere)

Today: allowed 1.0, limited 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.10 (low / mid / high), not allowed 0
Towns not in the list are treated as limited. This is an assumption. Many PA towns allow some kind of in-law unit, but the rules are not coded yet

Output: data/processed/forecast_town.csv

title: MUSA 6950 Proposal
text:
Submitted Nov 3, 2026.
Room for a Backyard Home: Measuring ADU Capacity Across Pennsylvania with GeoAI
Team: Ye Zhang
Background and Research Question: Pennsylvania needs more housing, but most towns make it hard to build an accessory dwelling unit (ADU), a small second home on a lot, like a backyard cottage. A state bill, HB 2186, would allow one on every home lot. But no one knows how many lots actually have room for one. Backyards also hold a lot of trees, so building there has an environmental cost.
Research question: How many home lots in Pennsylvania have room for a backyard ADU, how many could fit one without cutting down trees, and can AI on aerial images measure this better than building outlines alone?
Study Area: The whole state of Pennsylvania (all 67 counties), with results for every census tract, town, and county.
Goal: Builders and homeowners can type in an address and see if an ADU fits and where. Planners can see how many new homes ADUs could add in their town or county.
Data Sources: Aerial images of the whole state (NAIP, 2022), building outlines (Microsoft), and property lines from counties that share them. For training, I will use land cover maps from Philadelphia and the Chesapeake Bay area, plus a few hundred lots I label by hand.
Proposed AI Methods: First, a U-Net sorts each image into buildings, trees, and open ground, since building outlines alone do not show trees or pavement. I will compare it with a simpler Random Forest model. Second, YOLO finds garages and sheds the outlines miss. Third, a simple rule checks if each lot has an open spot big enough for an ADU, with and without cutting trees. I will test accuracy on lots I labeled myself, then run it statewide.
Expected Outcomes: A model that maps buildings, trees, and open ground; a map of how many lots can fit an ADU, with and without cutting trees; a check of how accurate the AI is; and a dashboard with an address search and a town and county view. I will share the results in a written report and a presentation.
About the Larger Project: This is half of a bigger ADU project. This half asks whether an ADU fits. My MUSA 5500 project asks whether people need housing there and whether an ADU would pay off, using population, job, and rent trends since 2010. Together they show whether there is room for ADUs where people need housing. Both will share one dashboard, but each class will have its own code and documentation.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text: Six steps. Each step is one notebook in musa6950/notebooks/.

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
section: 1. Look at the data and hand-label lots
text:
1. Look at the data and hand-label lots
Notebook 01_look_and_label.ipynb

Plot a few boxes: image next to label
Check class shares in train vs test
Pick 200-300 single-family lots in the test counties (Cumberland, Centre) and Philadelphia
For each lot, mark by eye: does a 20 x 30 ft (600 sq ft) spot fit in the backyard? With or without cutting trees?
Save as data/processed/hand_labels.csv (lot_id, fits, fits_keep_trees)
This is the ground truth for the last check
Done so far: plots and class shares. Hand labels are not made yet

Notebook 05 writes a blank form, hand_labels_template.csv: 250 random lots (seed 42), Philadelphia + Cumberland
Centre has no lot lines in this project, so it is not in the form

4 of the 177 boxes (on the New York line) have no 2022 PA image. 173 boxes are used: 146 train, 27 test

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
2. Random Forest baseline
Notebook 02_random_forest.ipynb (from Lab 6)

Each pixel = 4 band values (R, G, B, NIR) + NDVI
500 random pixels per class per box
RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100)
Score on the test counties: per-class IoU, mean IoU, confusion matrix
Every labeled pixel of the 27 test boxes is scored (about 109 million)

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
3. U-Net
Notebook 03_unet.ipynb (from Lab 9 and my Assignment 6)

Cut boxes into 256 x 256 tiles
4 input bands, 4 output classes (other, building, tree, open ground). 255 = ignore
Class-weighted cross entropy, Adam lr 0.001, batch 8
Random flips, same flip on image and label
Validation = a few train counties held back. Test = Cumberland + Centre

7 counties held back (seed 42), 24 boxes. 122 boxes left for training

What was run: plain U-Net written in torch (musa6950/unet.py), base width 32, 7.8 M parameters

Class weights = 1 / sqrt(class share)
Cosine decay of the learning rate over 10 epochs. 45 min on a Mac (MPS)
Best epoch by validation mIoU is kept
Test boxes are predicted in 512 px windows with a 64 px margin

Same scores as the Random Forest so they compare
Train on Mac (MPS) or Google Colab GPU
Note from Assignment 6: bare soil scored 0 IoU. Here bare ground is part of “open ground”

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
4. Garages and sheds (YOLO)
Notebook 04_sheds.ipynb (from Lab 8 and my Assignment 5)

Simple way first: inside each lot, the biggest building outline = the house. Other outlines under 60 m² = garage or shed
Then YOLO: label 150-300 sheds in LabelMe, convert to YOLO format, fine-tune
Does YOLO find sheds that the outlines miss?
YOLO (ultralytics) is AGPL. Keep it in this notebook only. The rest of the code never imports it
What was run: only the outline method. YOLO is not done (no shed labels yet). Left as an optional section
This notebook also picks the single-family lots for step 5

Philadelphia: lot building type starts with DET (detached). Rowhouses and twins are dropped. Microsoft merges a row into one outline, so the house can not be found
Cumberland: no building type in the lot file. Lots of 300-20,000 m2
Both: biggest outline on the lot is 60-600 m2 and no other outline is over 100 m2

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
section: 5. Room for an ADU (the fit rule)
text:
5. Room for an ADU (the fit rule)
Notebook 05_room_rule.ipynb

For each single-family lot in the pilot counties:

Backyard = lot minus house minus a setback buffer (try 5 ft from lot lines, 10 ft from the house)
Open = backyard pixels the model calls open ground
Fits = a 20 x 30 ft rectangle fits in the open area

Test with morphological erosion: erode the open mask by the rectangle. Any pixel left = fits
Try both rotations

Fits keeping trees = same test, but tree pixels are not allowed
Tree loss = tree area inside the spot when the only spot needs trees cut

Check against the hand labels from step 1: precision, recall
Compare: rule using only building outlines vs rule using the U-Net map
What was run, where it differs:

Work is in UTM 18N meters (the NAIP grid), not EPSG:2272. Same setbacks in meters. The rectangle is 10 x 15 pixels (6.0 x 9.0 m)
“Backyard” = the whole lot left after setbacks, front or back
Other outlines (garages, sheds) are taken out with no buffer
The erosion test is done with a summed-area table. Same answer, faster
NAIP for the pilot counties is read straight from Planetary Computer, only the 512 px blocks that touch a lot. Nothing is saved
Hand labels are not made yet, so there is no precision / recall against them
Instead: Cumberland lots inside the test boxes are run twice, with the Chesapeake label map and with the U-Net map. Agreement shows how much U-Net errors change the answer
open_m2 and tree_m2 in lots_pilot.csv are for the whole lot

title: MUSA 6950 Methods
text:
6. Statewide numbers
Notebook 06_statewide.ipynb

Fit rate = lots that fit / single-family lots, by urban / suburban / rural, from the pilot counties
Lots with room per tract = single-family detached homes (ACS B25024) x fit rate for that tract’s group
Range from bootstrap (resample lots 1,000 times)

What was run: resample whole tracts, not single lots, since lots next to each other are alike

Pilot lots by group: urban = Philadelphia + Cumberland urban tracts. Suburban and rural = Cumberland only
The group rate is used in every tract, the pilot counties too. The lot map has the per-lot answers
Tree loss per tract = lots_fit x mean tree area cut per fitting lot in the group
Output for the tool:

data/processed/lots_tract.csv (every tract)
data/processed/lots_pilot.csv (every lot in the pilot counties)
